lesson.title: The Nucleus Within the Nucleus: The Nucleolus and Ribosome Assembly
lesson.summary: The nucleolus is a dense, unmembraned region inside the nucleus dedicated to producing ribosomal RNA and assembling the two subunits that will become ribosomes.
lesson.body:
Inside the nucleus, viewed under a microscope, one region almost always stands out as noticeably darker and denser than the surrounding chromatin. This is the nucleolus, and unlike the nucleus itself, the nucleolus is not surrounded by its own membrane. It is instead a densely packed region that forms around specific stretches of DNA called nucleolar organizer regions, chromosomal segments that carry many repeated copies of the genes encoding ribosomal RNA. Because these genes are clustered together and transcribed at an extremely high rate, the region around them accumulates a dense concentration of RNA and protein that is visibly distinct from the rest of the nuclear interior, even without a membrane to mark its boundary.

The nucleolus's central job is building the two subunits that will eventually come together to form a functional ribosome. This begins with transcription of the ribosomal RNA genes, carried out by a dedicated form of RNA polymerase that operates almost exclusively within the nucleolus. The resulting ribosomal RNA is then processed and combined with ribosomal proteins that were synthesized separately out in the cytoplasm and imported back into the nucleus through the nuclear pore complexes described in the previous section, an example of exactly the kind of selective, signal-dependent nuclear import those pores are built to handle. Inside the nucleolus, ribosomal RNA and imported ribosomal proteins are assembled into the large and small ribosomal subunits.

Once assembled, the large and small subunits are exported separately back out through the nuclear pores into the cytoplasm, where they remain functionally incomplete until they encounter a molecule of messenger RNA. Only when a small subunit and a large subunit come together on an mRNA strand does a complete, functional ribosome exist, ready to carry out translation. The nucleolus, in other words, builds the components of the cell's protein-making machinery without ever actually running that machinery itself, since translation always takes place afterward, out in the cytoplasm.

Because ribosome production scales with how much protein synthesis a cell needs to perform, the size and prominence of the nucleolus varies considerably from one cell type to another and even within the same cell over time. Cells that are actively growing or that specialize in secreting large amounts of protein, such as cells in glands that produce digestive enzymes or hormones, tend to have unusually large, prominent nucleoli, reflecting the correspondingly heavy demand for freshly assembled ribosomes. A cell that is relatively quiescent and not synthesizing much protein typically shows a smaller, less conspicuous nucleolus.

The nucleolus is a useful reminder that not every functional structure inside a cell needs a membrane to stay organized. Its existence depends entirely on the ongoing, concentrated activity of transcribing ribosomal RNA genes and assembling ribosomal subunits at that one site, and it can even disperse and reform around the nucleolar organizer regions as this transcriptional activity rises and falls, particularly around cell division, when the nucleolus, like the rest of the nuclear architecture, is temporarily reorganized before reassembling in the daughter nuclei.
